rocket.definition: Any vehicle self-propelled by a rocket engine.

space-shuttle.definition: NASA’s space shuttle program managed a fleet of shuttles from 1981 through 2011. It organized launches, oversaw missions, and arranged maintenance.

satellite.definition: A machine sent into space to collect information and send it back.
satellite.exampleUsage: The satellite was used during the activity.

capsule.definition: A spacecraft designed to transport people and support human life in outer space.

lander.definition: A space vehicle that is designed to land on the moon or another planet.

rover.definition: A robotic vehicle designed to explore the surface of another world.

probe.definition: An inquiry into unfamiliar or questionable activities.

booster.definition: The first stage of a multistage rocket.

payload.definition: The equipment, cargo, or instruments carried by a rocket or spacecraft.

launch-pad.definition: A specially built platform where rockets or spacecraft begin their ascent.

sun.definition: The star that is the source of light and heat for the planets in the solar system.

mercury.definition: The smallest planet in the Solar System and the closest to the Sun.

venus.definition: The second nearest planet to the sun.

mars.definition: A small reddish planet that is the 4th from the sun and is periodically visible to the naked eye.

jupiter.definition: The largest planet and the 5th from the sun.

saturn.definition: A giant planet that is surrounded by three planar concentric rings of ice particles.

uranus.definition: A giant planet with a ring of ice particles.

neptune.definition: A giant planet with a ring of ice particles.

moon.definition: The natural satellite of the Earth.

asteroid.definition: Any of numerous small celestial bodies composed of rock and metal that move around the sun (mainly between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter).

comet.definition: (astronomy) a relatively small extraterrestrial body consisting of a frozen mass that travels around the sun in a highly elliptical orbit.

astronaut.definition: A person trained to travel in a spacecraft.

spacesuit.definition: A pressure suit worn by astronauts while in outer space.

helmet.definition: A hard covering worn to protect the head.

mission-control.definition: A facility where teams monitor, communicate with, and support spacecraft or space missions from the ground.
mission-control.exampleUsage: Mission control tracked the spacecraft throughout the test.

countdown.definition: Counting backward from an arbitrary number to indicate the time remaining before some event (such as launching a space vehicle).

liftoff.definition: The initial ascent of a rocket from its launching pad.

orbit.definition: The curved path one object follows around another in space.

spacewalk.definition: To move in space outside a space craft.

docking.definition: The joining of two spacecraft so they can operate or transfer people and supplies together.

re-entry.definition: The return of a spacecraft into a planet's atmosphere.

splashdown.definition: A landing of a spacecraft in the sea at the end of a space flight.

telescope.definition: An instrument that makes distant objects appear larger and easier to see.

star.definition: A luminous ball of hot gas that produces its own energy.

nebula.definition: An immense cloud of gas (mainly hydrogen) and dust in interstellar space.

black-hole.definition: A region of space forms when a massive star collapses, creating gravity so intense that nothing, not even light, can escape.

supernova.definition: A star that explodes and becomes extremely luminous in the process.

constellation.definition: A configuration of stars as seen from the earth.

meteor.definition: The bright streak seen when space debris enters an atmosphere and heats up.

aurora.definition: An atmospheric phenomenon consisting of bands of light caused by charged solar particles following the earth's magnetic lines of force.

eclipse.definition: An event in which one celestial object blocks light from another.

cosmic-dust.definition: Tiny solid grains found between and around stars and planets, made from materials such as rock, carbon, frozen substances, or metals.

solar-panel.definition: A device with linked semiconductor cells that changes sunlight directly into electrical power.
solar-panel.exampleUsage: The solar panel was used during the activity.

antenna.definition: A device that sends or receives radio and television signals.
antenna.exampleUsage: The antenna was used during the activity.

radar.definition: A system that uses radio waves to detect objects or weather.

computer.definition: A machine for performing calculations automatically.
computer.exampleUsage: The computer was used during the activity.

fuel-tank.definition: A strong container designed to store fuel for an engine, vehicle, or spacecraft system.
fuel-tank.exampleUsage: The cutaway model shows where the spacecraft fuel tank is located.

thruster.definition: A small rocket engine that provides the thrust needed to maneuver a spacecraft.

heat-shield.definition: A protective layer prevents a spacecraft from overheating as it reenters Earth’s atmosphere.

parachute.definition: A fabric canopy that slows the fall of a person or object through the air.

robotic-arm.definition: A mechanical arm controlled by a computer to move or handle objects.

laboratory.definition: A region resembling a laboratory inasmuch as it offers opportunities for observation and practice and experimentation.
